title.zh: 卷一 帝紀第一 高祖宣帝
title.raw: 卷一 帝紀第一 高祖宣帝 Volume 1 Annals 1: Emperor Xuan

sentences.zh: 宣皇帝諱懿，字仲達，河內溫縣孝敬里人，姓司馬氏。

translations.literal: Emperor Xuan's taboo name was Yi; his courtesy name was Zhongda. He was a native of Xiaojing Ward in Wen County in the interior of Hedong, and his surname was Sima.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Xuan was posthumously styled Yi; he used the courtesy name Zhongda. He came from Xiaojing Ward in Wen County in Hedong Commandery and belonged to the house of Sima.

sentences.zh: 其先出自帝高陽之子重黎，為夏官祝融。

translations.literal: His ancestors traced their line to Chongli, son of Emperor Gaoyang (Zhuanxu), who held the office of Zhurong under the Xia.
translations.idiomatic: The line descended from Chongli, son of Zhuanxu, who served as Zhurong in the Ministry of Xia.

sentences.zh: 歷唐、虞、夏、商，世序其職。

translations.literal: Through the eras of Tang, Yu, Xia, and Shang, generation after generation they succeeded one another in that office.
translations.idiomatic: Across Tang, Yu, Xia, and Shang, his forebears held that post in unbroken succession.

sentences.zh: 及周，以夏官為司馬。

translations.literal: Under the Zhou, the Xia ministry was styled Marshal (Sima).
translations.idiomatic: When the Zhou reorganized the bureaucracy, the old Xia office became the Ministry of the Marshal.

sentences.zh: 其後程伯休父，周宣王時，以世官克平徐方，錫以官族，因而為氏。

translations.literal: Later Cheng Bo Xiufu, in the reign of King Xuan of Zhou, by virtue of his hereditary office conquered and pacified the Xu lands and was granted a clan name taken from his office; his descendants therefore took Sima as their surname.
translations.idiomatic: Later, Cheng Bo Xiufu—during King Xuan of Zhou—used his hereditary charge to crush the Xu region and received a clan designation from his title; from that the Sima surname arose.

sentences.zh: 楚漢間，司馬卬為趙將，與諸侯伐秦。

translations.literal: Between Chu and Han, Sima Ang served as a Zhao general and joined the feudal lords in attacking Qin.
translations.idiomatic: In the turmoil between Chu and Han, Sima Ang commanded troops for Zhao and marched with the alliance against Qin.

sentences.zh: 秦亡，立為殷王，都河內。

translations.literal: When Qin fell, [Ang] was established as King of Yin and made his capital in Henei.
translations.idiomatic: After Qin collapsed he was enthroned as king of Yin with his seat at Henei.

sentences.zh: 漢以其地為郡，子孫遂家焉。

translations.literal: Han converted his territory into a commandery, and his descendants settled there.
translations.idiomatic: The Han turned that territory into a commandery, and his line took root there.

sentences.zh: 自卬八世，生征西將軍鈞，字叔平。

translations.literal: Eight generations after Ang was born General Who Guards the West Jun, courtesy name Shuping.
translations.idiomatic: Eight generations down from Ang came General Who Guards the West Jun, whose courtesy name was Shuping.

sentences.zh: 鈞生豫章太守量，字公度。

translations.literal: Jun fathered Prefect of Yuzhang Liang, courtesy name Gongdu.
translations.idiomatic: Jun’s son was Liang, prefect of Yuzhang, courtesy name Gongdu.

sentences.zh: 量生潁川太守儁，字元異。

translations.literal: Liang fathered Prefect of Yingchuan Jun, courtesy name Yuanyi.
translations.idiomatic: Liang’s son was Jun, prefect of Yingchuan, courtesy name Yuanyi.

sentences.zh: 儁生京兆尹防，字建公。

translations.literal: Jun fathered Governor of the Metropolitan Region Fang, courtesy name Jiangong.
translations.idiomatic: Jun’s son was Fang, governor of Jingzhao, courtesy name Jiangong.

sentences.zh: 帝即防之第二子也。

translations.literal: The Emperor was Fang’s second son.
translations.idiomatic: He was the second son of Fang.

sentences.zh: 少有奇節，聰朗多大略，博學洽聞，伏膺儒教。

translations.literal: In youth he showed uncommon integrity; he was bright and broad in strategic grasp, widely read and well informed, and devoted himself to Confucian teaching.
translations.idiomatic: Even young he revealed unusual steadfastness—acute, far-sighted, erudite, and steeped in the Confucian canon.

sentences.zh: 漢末大亂，常慨然有憂天下心。

translations.literal: At the end of Han, when great turmoil arose, he often felt stirred with concern for the realm.
translations.idiomatic: As Han unraveled, he was repeatedly consumed by anxiety for the empire.

sentences.zh: 南陽太守同郡楊俊名知人，[1]見帝，未弱冠，以為非常之器。

translations.literal: Yang Jun of the same commandery, prefect of Nanyang, famed for judging men,[1] met the Emperor before his twentieth year and deemed him an extraordinary vessel.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Jun of Nanyang—his fellow townsman and a celebrated judge of talent—met him before his cap-and-girdle ceremony and pronounced him a figure of rare promise.

sentences.zh: 尚書清河崔琰與帝兄朗善，亦謂朗曰：「君弟聰亮明允，剛斷英特，非子所及也。」

translations.literal: Minister Cui Yan of Qinghe was on good terms with the Emperor’s elder brother Lang and also said to Lang, “Your younger brother is clear-sighted and fair-minded, resolute and extraordinary—not someone you can match.”
translations.idiomatic: Cui Yan of Qinghe, who served in the Secretariat, was close to his elder brother Sima Lang and told Lang, “Your brother combines lucidity with integrity and carries an iron decisiveness—you cannot rival him.”

sentences.zh: 漢建安六年，郡舉上計掾。

translations.literal: In the sixth year of Jian’an of Han, the commandery nominated him as clerk for the annual accounts.
translations.idiomatic: In Han’s sixth Jian’an year the commandery recommended him as clerk for the capital assessment.

sentences.zh: 魏武帝為司空，聞而辟之。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu of Wei was Minister of Works and, hearing of him, summoned him.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao, then Minister of Works for Wei, heard of him and ordered him to take office.

sentences.zh: 帝知漢運方微，不欲屈節曹氏，辭以風痹，不能起居。

translations.literal: The Emperor knew Han’s mandate was failing and did not wish to bend his integrity to the Cao house; he declined on the grounds of wind paralysis and inability to rise.
translations.idiomatic: Knowing the Han house was spent, he refused to humble himself before the Caos and pleaded crippling wind paralysis that kept him from rising.

sentences.zh: 魏武使人夜往密刺之，帝堅臥不動。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu sent someone by night to stab him secretly; the Emperor lay rigid and did not move.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao sent an assassin in the dark; he stayed rigidly abed and never stirred.

sentences.zh: 及魏武為丞相，又辟為文學掾，敕行者曰：「若復盤桓，便收之。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wu became Chancellor, he again summoned him as clerk for literature and instructed the messenger: “If he stalls again, arrest him.”
translations.idiomatic: When Cao Cao became Chancellor he summoned him again as literary clerk and told the courier, “If he hesitates once more, seize him.”

sentences.zh: 」帝懼而就職。

translations.literal: The Emperor, in fear, took the post.
translations.idiomatic: Terrified, he accepted the appointment.

sentences.zh: 於是使與太子游處，遷黃門侍郎，轉議郎、丞相東曹屬，尋轉主簿。

translations.literal: He was then assigned to associate with the heir apparent; he rose to Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates, transferred to Consultant, aide in the Chancellor’s eastern bureau, and soon became chief clerk.
translations.idiomatic: Thereafter he attended the heir apparent, advanced to gentleman at the Yellow Gates, moved through Consultant and aide in the Chancellor’s eastern department, and shortly became chief clerk.

sentences.zh: 從討張魯，言於魏武曰：「劉備以詐力虜劉璋，蜀人未附而遠爭江陵，此機不可失也。

translations.literal: Accompanying the campaign against Zhang Lu, he said to Emperor Wu, “Liu Bei seized Liu Zhang by deceit and force; the people of Shu are not yet attached, yet he contests Jiangling from afar—this opportunity must not be missed.”
translations.idiomatic: On the expedition against Zhang Lu he urged Cao Cao: “Liu Bei bullied his way into Yi through trickery; the Shu populace still mistrusts him while he reaches for Jiangling—do not let this opening slip.”

sentences.zh: 今若曜威漢中，益州震動，進兵臨之，勢必瓦解。

translations.literal: “If we now display our might in Hanzhong, Yizhou will be shaken; advance the army against it and it will surely crumble.
translations.idiomatic: “Show strength in Hanzhong and Yi province will reel; press forward and their front will collapse.”

sentences.zh: 因此之勢，易為功力。

translations.literal: Riding this momentum, success will come easily.
translations.idiomatic: Ride that tide and the task becomes straightforward.”

sentences.zh: 聖人不能違時，亦不失時矣。

translations.literal: The sage cannot defy the hour, yet neither does he miss it.”
translations.idiomatic: Even the sage neither fights the moment nor lets it pass unused.”

sentences.zh: 」魏武曰：「人苦無足，既得隴右，復欲得蜀！

translations.literal: Emperor Wu said, “Men suffer from insatiable greed—having gained Longyou, they want Shu too!”
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao replied, “People are never satisfied—take Longyou and they hunger for Shu!”

sentences.zh: 」言竟不從。

translations.literal: In the end he did not follow the advice.
translations.idiomatic: He would not take the counsel.

sentences.zh: 既而從討孫權，破之。

translations.literal: He then accompanied the campaign against Sun Quan and defeated him.
translations.idiomatic: He later joined the campaign against Sun Quan and helped rout him.

sentences.zh: 軍還，權遣使乞降，上表稱臣，陳說天命。

translations.literal: When the army returned, Sun Quan sent envoys begging to surrender, submitted a memorial declaring himself a subject, and expounded the mandate of Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: On the army’s return Sun Quan sent envoys suing for peace, presented a memorial as a vassal, and rehearsed Heaven’s mandate.

sentences.zh: 魏武帝曰：「此兒欲踞吾著爐炭上邪！

translations.literal: Emperor Wu of Wei said, “Does this fellow want to seat me on coals over a furnace?”
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao snapped, “Does that boy mean to roast me over live coals?”

sentences.zh: 」答曰：「漢運垂終，殿下十分天下而有其九，以服事之。

translations.literal: He replied: “Han’s mandate is near its end; Your Highness holds nine-tenths of the realm yet still serves it.
translations.idiomatic: He answered: “The Han flame gutters while you hold nine parts in ten yet still bow to the emperor.

sentences.zh: 權之稱臣，天人之意也。

translations.literal: Sun Quan’s submission accords with the will of Heaven and men.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan’s offer to submit answers both Heaven and the human heart.

sentences.zh: 虞、夏、殷、周不以謙讓者，畏天知命也。」

translations.literal: Yu, Xia, Yin, and Zhou did not yield out of mere modesty—they feared Heaven and knew the mandate.”
translations.idiomatic: The sage-kings of Yu, Xia, Shang, and Zhou yielded not from timidity but because they revered Heaven and accepted its mandate.”

sentences.zh: 魏國既建，遷太子中庶子。

translations.literal: When the state of Wei was established, he was promoted to palace attendant to the heir apparent.
translations.idiomatic: Once the Wei kingdom was founded he rose to palace attendant to the heir apparent.

sentences.zh: 每與大謀，輒有奇策，為太子所信重，與陳羣、吳質、朱鑠號曰四友。

translations.literal: Whenever major plans were laid he produced striking stratagems; the heir trusted and esteemed him, and with Chen Qun, Wu Zhi, and Zhu Shuo he was called the Four Friends.
translations.idiomatic: In every grand council he supplied sharp schemes; the heir relied on him and paired him with Chen Qun, Wu Zhi, and Zhu Shuo as the “Four Friends.”

sentences.zh: 遷為軍司馬，言於魏武曰：「昔箕子陳謀，以食為首。

translations.literal: He was promoted to army marshal and said to Emperor Wu, “When Jizi presented his counsel, he put food first.
translations.idiomatic: Promoted army marshal, he told Cao Cao: “When Jizi advised the king, grain came first.

sentences.zh: 今天下不耕者蓋二十餘萬，非經國遠籌也。

translations.literal: Today perhaps two hundred thousand men do not till the soil—this is no far-reaching policy for governing the state.”
translations.idiomatic: Today perhaps two hundred thousand arms lie idle from the plough—that is no blueprint for ruling the realm.”

sentences.zh: 雖戎甲未卷，自宜且耕且守。

translations.literal: Though armor is not yet laid aside, we should farm and defend at the same time.”
translations.idiomatic: War gear may still be buckled on, yet we must sow while we guard.”

sentences.zh: 」魏武納之，於是務農積穀，國用豐贍。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu accepted this; agriculture was emphasized and grain stored, and state supplies grew ample.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao agreed; farming and granaries were stressed until state stores overflowed.

sentences.zh: 帝又言荊州刺史胡脩粗暴，南鄉太守傅方驕奢，並不可居邊。

translations.literal: The Emperor also said that Hu Xiu, inspector of Jingzhou, was brutal and coarse, and Fu Fang, prefect of Nanxiang, arrogant and extravagant—neither was fit to hold the frontier.
translations.idiomatic: He further warned that Hu Xiu, inspector of Jingzhou, was brutish and Fu Fang, prefect of Nanxiang, was decadent—neither belonged on the border.

sentences.zh: 魏武不之察。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu did not heed him.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao brushed the warning aside.

sentences.zh: 及蜀將關羽圍曹仁於樊，于禁等七軍皆沒，脩、方果降羽，而仁圍甚急焉。

translations.literal: When Shu general Guan Yu besieged Cao Ren at Fan and Yu Jin’s seven armies were drowned, Hu and Fu indeed surrendered to Guan Yu, and Ren’s siege grew desperate.
translations.idiomatic: When Guan Yu of Shu penned Cao Ren at Fan and Yu Jin’s seven corps vanished beneath the flood, Hu Xiu and Fu Fang duly defected to Guan Yu and the siege of Fan tightened unbearably.

sentences.zh: 是時漢帝都許昌，魏武以為近賊，欲徙河北。

translations.literal: At that time the Han emperor was at Xuchang; Emperor Wu thought it too close to the enemy and wished to move the capital north of the Yellow River.
translations.idiomatic: The Han emperor still sat at Xuchang; Cao Cao judged it perilously near the foe and planned to shift the court north of the river.

sentences.zh: 帝諫曰：「禁等為水所沒，非戰守之所失，於國家大計未有所損，而便遷都，既示敵以弱，又淮沔之人大不安矣。

translations.literal: The Emperor remonstrated: “Yu Jin and the others were lost to water, not to defeat in battle or defense—the state’s grand plan is not yet harmed. To move the capital rashly would show weakness to the enemy and greatly unsettle the people between the Huai and the Han.
translations.idiomatic: He objected: “Yu Jin’s men drowned—they were not routed in the field. The empire’s strategy is intact; relocating now advertises fear and panics everyone between the Huai and the Han.

sentences.zh: 孫權、劉備，外親內疏，羽之得意，權所不願也。

translations.literal: Sun Quan and Liu Bei are outward kin but inwardly estranged; Guan Yu’s triumph is not what Quan desires.”
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan and Liu Bei are allies in name alone; Sun Quan cannot relish Guan Yu’s triumph.”

sentences.zh: 可喻權所，令掎其後，則樊圍自解。

translations.literal: You may instruct Quan to strike Guan Yu from behind; then the siege of Fan will lift of itself.”
translations.idiomatic: Urge Sun Quan to stab Guan Yu in the rear and the ring around Fan loosens on its own.”

sentences.zh: 」魏武從之。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu followed this advice.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao adopted the plan.

sentences.zh: 權果遣將呂蒙西襲公安，拔之，羽遂為蒙所獲。

translations.literal: Quan indeed sent general Lü Meng to raid Gong’an from the west and took it; Guan Yu was then captured by Meng.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan dispatched Lü Meng westward against Gong’an, seized it, and Guan Yu fell into Meng’s hands.

sentences.zh: 魏武以荊州遺黎及屯田在潁川者逼近南寇，[2]皆欲徙之。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu wished to relocate the remnant people of Jingzhou and the agricultural colonies in Yingchuan because they lay close to the southern foe.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao meant to uproot the leftover households of Jingzhou and the military colonies in Yingchuan because both fronts skirted the southern enemy.

sentences.zh: 帝曰：「荊楚輕脫，易動難安。

translations.literal: The Emperor said, “The people of Jing-Chu are flighty—easy to stir, hard to settle.
translations.idiomatic: He replied, “The Jing-Chu folk are restless—quick to bolt and slow to reassure.

sentences.zh: 關羽新破，諸為惡者藏竄觀望。

translations.literal: Guan Yu has just been defeated; those who meant harm hide and watch.”
translations.idiomatic: Guan Yu’s fall leaves malcontents skulking in the shadows, watching.”

sentences.zh: 今徙其善者，既傷其意，將令去者不敢復還。

translations.literal: If we now relocate the good among them, we wound their feelings and will make those who flee dare not return.”
translations.idiomatic: Uproot the loyal now and you crush their hearts; refugees will never dare come home.”

sentences.zh: 」從之。

translations.literal: [Emperor Wu] followed this.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao relented.

sentences.zh: 其後諸亡者悉復業。

translations.literal: Afterwards all who had fled resumed their occupations.
translations.idiomatic: Later every exile drifted back to his fields.

sentences.zh: 及魏武薨于洛陽，朝野危懼。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wu died at Luoyang, court and countryside were fearful.
translations.idiomatic: When Cao Cao died at Luoyang, court and capital trembled.

sentences.zh: 帝綱紀喪事，內外肅然。

translations.literal: The Emperor directed the funeral rites; within and without there was solemn order.
translations.idiomatic: He imposed discipline on the mourning rites until palace and province stood calm.

sentences.zh: 乃奉梓宮還鄴。

translations.literal: He then escorted the coffin back to Ye.
translations.idiomatic: He convoyed the royal catafalque back to Ye.

sentences.zh: 黃初二年，督軍官罷，遷侍中、尚書右僕射。

translations.literal: In the second year of Huangchu (221), the office of supervisor of armies was abolished; he was promoted to palace attendant and right vice director of the Secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: In Huangchu’s second year the army-supervisor post was scrapped; he became palace attendant and right vice director of the Secretariat.

sentences.zh: 五年，天子南巡，觀兵吳疆。

translations.literal: In the fifth year (224), the Son of Heaven toured south and reviewed troops on Wu’s border.
translations.idiomatic: In the fifth year the emperor toured south and drilled troops along Wu’s frontier.

sentences.zh: 帝留鎮許昌，改封向鄉侯，轉撫軍、假節，領兵五千，加給事中、錄尚書事。

translations.literal: The Emperor remained to guard Xuchang, was enfeoffed as marquis of Xiangxiang, became Protector of the Army with ceremonial axe, commanded five thousand troops, and was given concurrent posts as attendant within the palace and recorder of Secretariat affairs.
translations.idiomatic: He stayed to hold Xuchang, was refeoffed marquis of Xiang township, promoted Protector of the Army with credential axe, led five thousand soldiers, and added duties as palace attendant and overseer of Secretariat business.

sentences.zh: 帝固辭。

translations.literal: The Emperor firmly declined.
translations.idiomatic: He firmly declined.

sentences.zh: 天子曰：「吾於庶事，以夜繼晝，無須臾寧息。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven said, “In routine affairs I follow night with day without a moment’s rest.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor said, “I chase paperwork from dusk to dawn without a breath’s pause.

sentences.zh: 此非以為榮，乃分憂耳。」

translations.literal: This is not for honor—it is to share my burdens.”
translations.idiomatic: That burden is not glory—it is sharing the weight on my shoulders.”

sentences.zh: 六年，天子復大興舟師征吳，復命帝居守，內鎮百姓，外供軍資。

translations.literal: In the sixth year (225), the Son of Heaven again raised a great fleet to campaign against Wu and again ordered the Emperor to remain as guardian—pacifying the people within and supplying the army without.
translations.idiomatic: The sixth year brought another massive river expedition against Wu; again he was told to stay behind—steady the interior and provision the campaign.

sentences.zh: 臨行，詔曰：「吾深以後事為念，故以委卿。

translations.literal: On departure he issued an edict: “I think deeply on what comes after me; therefore I entrust you.
translations.idiomatic: Before embarking he proclaimed: “I brood over what follows my reign—so I lay it in your hands.

sentences.zh: 曹參雖有戰功，而蕭何為重。

translations.literal: Cao Can had battle merit, yet Xiao He mattered more.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Can won battles, yet Xiao He anchored the state.

sentences.zh: 使吾無西顧之憂，不亦可乎！

translations.literal: Let me have no worry over the west—is that not enough!”
translations.idiomatic: Free my mind from the western march—is that too much to ask!”

sentences.zh: 」天子自廣陵還洛陽，詔帝曰：「吾東，撫軍當總西事；

translations.literal: When the Son of Heaven returned from Guangling to Luoyang, he edicted the Emperor: “When I am east, the Protector of the Army shall oversee the west;
translations.idiomatic: Returning from Guangling to Luoyang he decreed: “When I march east, the Protector commands the west;

sentences.zh: 吾西，撫軍當總東事。

translations.literal: when I am west, the Protector of the Army shall oversee the east.”
translations.idiomatic: when I march west, the Protector commands the east.”

sentences.zh: 」於是帝留鎮許昌。

translations.literal: Thereupon the Emperor remained to guard Xuchang.
translations.idiomatic: So he continued to anchor Xuchang.

sentences.zh: 及孫權圍江夏，遣其將諸葛瑾、張霸并攻襄陽，帝督諸軍討權，走之。

translations.literal: When Sun Quan besieged Jiangxia and sent his generals Zhuge Jin and Zhang Ba jointly to attack Xiangyang, the Emperor commanded the armies against Quan and drove him off.
translations.idiomatic: When Sun Quan invested Jiangxia and Zhuge Jin with Zhang Ba struck Xiangyang together, he led the host against Sun Quan and threw him back.

sentences.zh: 進擊，敗瑾，斬霸，并首級千餘。

translations.literal: Pressing the attack, he defeated Jin, beheaded Ba, and took over a thousand heads.
translations.idiomatic: He pressed the pursuit, routed Zhuge Jin, slew Zhang Ba, and piled up more than a thousand heads.

sentences.zh: 遷驃騎將軍。

translations.literal: He was promoted to general of agile cavalry.
translations.idiomatic: He was elevated to general of the agile cavalry.

sentences.zh: 太和元年六月，天子詔帝屯于宛，加督荊、豫二州諸軍事。

translations.literal: In the sixth month of the first year of Taihe (227), the Son of Heaven ordered the Emperor to encamp at Wan and added command of military affairs in Jing and Yu provinces.
translations.idiomatic: Taihe’s first year, sixth month: the court ordered him to camp at Wan and added authority over all troops in Jing and Yu.

sentences.zh: 初，蜀將孟達之降也，魏朝遇之甚厚。

translations.literal: Earlier, when Shu general Meng Da had surrendered, the Wei court treated him generously.
translations.idiomatic: Earlier, when Shu’s general Meng Da defected, Wei showered him with favor.

sentences.zh: 帝以達言行傾巧不可任，驟諫不見聽，乃以達領新城太守，封侯，假節。

translations.literal: The Emperor deemed Da’s words and conduct slippery and unreliable; though he remonstrated repeatedly he was not heard, and Da was made acting prefect of Xincheng, enfeoffed as a marquis, and given the ceremonial axe.
translations.idiomatic: He judged Da’s tongue treacherous and untrustworthy; repeated remonstrance failed, so Da received acting prefect of Xincheng, a marquisate, and the credential axe.

sentences.zh: 達於是連吳固蜀，潛圖中國。

translations.literal: Da then allied with Wu and Shu and secretly plotted against the central plains.
translations.idiomatic: Da then stitched Wu to Shu and schemed against the heartland in secret.

sentences.zh: 蜀相諸葛亮惡其反覆，又慮其為患。

translations.literal: Shu’s chancellor Zhuge Liang despised his vacillation and also feared he would cause trouble.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuge Liang despised his flip-flopping and dreaded the chaos he might unleash.

sentences.zh: 達與魏興太守申儀有隙，亮欲促其事，乃遣郭模詐降，過儀，因漏泄其謀。

translations.literal: Da had a rift with Shen Yi, prefect of Weixing; Liang wished to hasten matters and sent Guo Mo feigning surrender, who passed through Yi and leaked the plot.
translations.idiomatic: Da quarrelled with Shen Yi of Weixing; Liang hurried matters by sending Guo Mo under false colors past Yi to spill the conspiracy.

sentences.zh: 達聞其謀漏泄，將舉兵。

translations.literal: When Da heard his plot had leaked, he prepared to rise in arms.
translations.idiomatic: Once Da learned the secret was out, he prepared to rebel.

sentences.zh: 帝恐達速發，以書喻之曰：「將軍昔棄劉備，託身國家，國家委將軍以疆埸之任，任將軍以圖蜀之事，可謂心貫白日。

translations.literal: The Emperor feared Da would move quickly and wrote to him: “General, you once abandoned Liu Bei and entrusted yourself to the state; the state entrusted you with the frontier and charged you with planning against Shu—your heart may be said to pierce the bright sun.
translations.idiomatic: Fearing a swift rising, he wrote: “You abandoned Liu Bei for us; we placed the border in your hands and tasked you with Shu—your loyalty blazes like noon.

sentences.zh: 蜀人愚智，莫不切齒於將軍。

translations.literal: Wise or foolish, everyone in Shu gnashes teeth at you.”
translations.idiomatic: Every Shu soul, wise or dull, grinds teeth at your name.”

sentences.zh: 諸葛亮欲相破，惟苦無路耳。

translations.literal: Zhuge Liang wishes to destroy you but only lacks the means.”
translations.idiomatic: Zhuge Liang longs to ruin you yet lacked a lever until now.”

sentences.zh: 模之所言，非小事也，亮豈輕之而令宣露，此殆易知耳。

translations.literal: What Mo said is no trifle—would Liang treat it lightly and let it spread? This is easy to see.”
translations.idiomatic: Mo’s tale is no gossip—would Zhuge Liang broadcast it carelessly? The answer is plain.”

sentences.zh: 」達得書大喜，猶與不決。

translations.literal: Da received the letter and was greatly pleased, yet still hesitated.
translations.idiomatic: Da read the letter with delight yet still wavered.

sentences.zh: 帝乃潛軍進討。

translations.literal: The Emperor then secretly advanced to attack.
translations.idiomatic: He then stole forward with the army.

sentences.zh: 諸將言達與二賊交構，宜觀望而後動。

translations.literal: The generals said Da was in league with the two foes and they should watch and wait before acting.
translations.idiomatic: His officers argued Da colluded with both enemies and urged caution.

sentences.zh: 帝曰：「達無信義，此其相疑之時也，當及其未定促決之。

translations.literal: The Emperor said, “Da lacks good faith; this is when mutual suspicion reigns—we must strike before he is settled.”
translations.idiomatic: He said, “Da knows no loyalty—this is the hour of mutual doubt; strike before his camp steadies.”

sentences.zh: 」乃倍道兼行，八日到其城下。

translations.literal: He therefore doubled the march and in eight days reached the walls.
translations.idiomatic: He forced the march and reached the walls in eight days.

sentences.zh: 吳蜀各遣其將向西城安橋、木闌塞以救達，帝分諸將以距之。

translations.literal: Wu and Shu each sent generals toward Xicheng, Anqiao, and Mulansai to relieve Da; the Emperor divided his generals to block them.
translations.idiomatic: Wu and Shu each rushed columns toward Xicheng, An Bridge, and Mulansai to rescue Da; he split commands to intercept them.

sentences.zh: 初，達與亮書曰：「宛去洛八百里，去吾一千二百里，聞吾舉事，當表上天子，比相反覆，一月間也，則吾城已固，諸軍足辦。

translations.literal: Earlier Da had written to Liang: “Wan is eight hundred li from Luoyang and twelve hundred from me; when I rise, [the court] must memorialize the Son of Heaven—by the time reports go back and forth a month will have passed; then my city will be secure and my forces ready.
translations.idiomatic: Da once wrote Zhuge Liang: “Wan lies eight hundred li from Luoyang and twelve hundred from me; were I to rebel, Luoyang must memorialize the throne—round-trip paperwork eats a month; by then my walls would stand firm and my troops ready.

sentences.zh: 則吾所在深險，司馬公必不自來；

translations.literal: My position is deep and defensible; Lord Sima will surely not come himself;
translations.idiomatic: My terrain is rugged and remote—Lord Sima will never march in person;

sentences.zh: 諸將來，吾無患矣。

translations.literal: if only his generals come, I have nothing to fear.”
translations.idiomatic: if only subordinates arrive I need not worry.”

sentences.zh: 」及兵到，達又告亮曰：「吾舉事八日，而兵至城下，何其神速也！

translations.literal: When the troops arrived, Da told Liang: “I rose eight days ago and already troops are at my walls—how swift!”
translations.idiomatic: When the army appeared Da wired Liang: “Eight days into my rising and they ring my walls—what speed!”

sentences.zh: 」上庸城三面阻水，達於城外為木柵以自固。

translations.literal: Shangyong was bounded by water on three sides; Da built a wooden palisade outside the city to fortify himself.
translations.idiomatic: Shangyong hugged water on three faces; Da threw up timber palisades beyond the walls.

sentences.zh: [3]帝渡水，破其柵，直造城下。

translations.literal: [3] The Emperor crossed the water, broke the palisade, and came straight to the foot of the walls.
translations.idiomatic: [3] He forded the streams, smashed the stockade, and drove to the moat.

sentences.zh: 八道攻之，旬有六日，達甥鄧賢、將李輔等開門出降。

translations.literal: He attacked from eight directions; after sixteen days Deng Xian, Da’s nephew, and general Li Fu and others opened the gates and surrendered.
translations.idiomatic: He assaulted along eight avenues; sixteen days later Deng Xian the nephew and general Li Fu opened the gates and capitulated.

sentences.zh: 斬達，傳首京師。

translations.literal: Da was executed and his head sent to the capital.
translations.idiomatic: They beheaded Meng Da and forwarded his head to Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 俘獲萬餘人，振旅還于宛。

translations.literal: More than ten thousand captives were taken; the army marched back to Wan in good order.
translations.idiomatic: They took over ten thousand prisoners and marched back to Wan with drums beating.

sentences.zh: 乃勸農桑，禁浮費，南土悅附焉。

translations.literal: He then promoted farming and sericulture, forbade wasteful spending, and the southern lands gladly submitted.
translations.idiomatic: He urged tillage and silk production, banned needless expense, and the south rallied to him willingly.

sentences.zh: 初，申儀久在魏興，專威疆埸，輒承制刻印，多所假授。

translations.literal: Earlier, Shen Yi had long held Weixing, arrogated authority along the frontier, repeatedly carved seals on his own authority, and handed out many irregular appointments.
translations.idiomatic: Shen Yi had dominated Weixing for years—running the border like a private fief, minting seals without sanction, and handing out titles at will.

sentences.zh: 達既誅，有自疑心。

translations.literal: After Da was put to death, Yi grew suspicious of his own position.
translations.idiomatic: Once Meng Da fell, Shen Yi began to doubt his own safety.

sentences.zh: 時諸郡守以帝新克捷，奉禮求賀，皆聽之。

translations.literal: At that time the various prefects, because the Emperor had just won a victory, brought gifts seeking congratulation; he accepted them all.
translations.idiomatic: County governors arrived with congratulations on his fresh triumph; he received every delegation.

sentences.zh: 帝使人諷儀，儀至，問承制狀，執之，歸于京師。

translations.literal: The Emperor sent someone to sound out Yi; when Yi came to court he questioned him about his unauthorized appointments, seized him, and sent him to the capital.
translations.idiomatic: He hinted until Shen Yi appeared at audience, pressed him on those self-made commissions, arrested him, and shipped him east.

sentences.zh: 又徙孟達餘眾七千餘家於幽州。

translations.literal: He also relocated more than seven thousand households of Meng Da’s remnant followers to Youzhou.
translations.idiomatic: He resettled over seven thousand surviving households of Meng Da’s clan in Youzhou.

sentences.zh: 蜀將姚靜、鄭他等帥其屬七千餘人來降。

translations.literal: Shu generals Yao Jing and Zheng Ta led their followers—more than seven thousand men—to surrender.
translations.idiomatic: Yao Jing and Zheng Ta of Shu marched in over seven thousand troops to defect.

sentences.zh: 時邊郡新附，多無戶名，魏朝欲加隱實。

translations.literal: At that time the newly annexed marches often lacked registered households, and the Wei court wished to verify them thoroughly.
translations.idiomatic: The newly subdued border prefectures still lacked proper household rolls, and the court meant to audit them.

sentences.zh: 屬帝朝於京師，天子訪之於帝。

translations.literal: When the Emperor attended court in the capital, the Son of Heaven consulted him on the matter.
translations.idiomatic: While he was at audience in Luoyang, the emperor took him aside for advice.

sentences.zh: 帝對曰：「賊以密網束下，故下棄之。

translations.literal: The Emperor replied: “The rebels bound their subjects with a harsh net, so the people abandoned them.
translations.idiomatic: He answered: “Bandits rule through a thousand petty regulations—that is why their subjects flee.

sentences.zh: 宜弘以大綱，則自然安樂。

translations.literal: You should rule with a broad policy; then peace will come of itself.”
translations.idiomatic: Govern with a loose rein and calm follows without forcing it.”

sentences.zh: 」又問二虜宜討，何者為先？

translations.literal: He was also asked which of the two enemies ought to be attacked first.
translations.idiomatic: The sovereign then asked which foe—Wu or Shu—should come first.

sentences.zh: 對曰：「吳以中國不習水戰，故敢散居東關。

translations.literal: He replied: “Wu presumes that the Central Plains do not excel at river warfare, which is why they dare scatter their forces along Dongguan.”
translations.idiomatic: He said: “Wu gambles that we fear naval combat, so they string their lines along the eastern passes.”

sentences.zh: 凡攻敵，必扼其喉而摏其心。

translations.literal: In every attack on an enemy one must seize his throat and strike his heart.”
translations.idiomatic: Strike always at throat and heart—that is how wars are won.”

sentences.zh: 夏口、東關，賊之心喉。

translations.literal: Xiakou and Dongguan are that foe’s heart and throat.”
translations.idiomatic: Xiakou and Dongguan are precisely those vital points.”

sentences.zh: 若為陸軍以向皖城，引權東下，為水戰軍向夏口，乘其虛而擊之，此神兵從天而墮，破之必矣。

translations.literal: If you march a field army toward Wancheng and draw Sun Quan eastward, while a river force pushes toward Xiakou and hits him where he is weak, it will be like heavenly troops falling from the sky—you will surely break him.”
translations.idiomatic: Send infantry toward Wancheng to tug Sun Quan downstream while your fleet thrusts at Xiakou and catches him thin—that is an assault from heaven itself.”

sentences.zh: 」天子並然之，復命帝屯於宛。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven deeply approved and again ordered the Emperor to encamp at Wan.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor endorsed it wholeheartedly and told him once more to hold Wan.

sentences.zh: 四年，遷大將軍，加大都督、假黃鉞，與曹真伐蜀。

translations.literal: In the fourth year he was promoted to Grand General, invested as supreme commander-in-chief with the yellow battle-axe, and joined Cao Zhen in campaigning against Shu.
translations.idiomatic: Fourth year: he became Grand General and supreme commander with the yellow axe, campaigning beside Cao Zhen against Shu.

sentences.zh: 帝自西城斫山開道，水陸並進，泝沔而上，至於朐䏰，拔其新豐縣。

translations.literal: From Xicheng he cut roads through the mountains and advanced by land and water together, moving up the Han River as far as Quyu, where he took Xinfeng County.
translations.idiomatic: He hacked a route from Xicheng, drove land and river columns up the Han to Quyu, and seized Xinfeng County.

sentences.zh: 軍次丹口，遇雨，班師。

translations.literal: The army halted at Dankou; rain fell and he ordered the troops withdrawn.
translations.idiomatic: They paused at Dankou until storms forced a withdrawal.

sentences.zh: 明年，諸葛亮寇天水，圍將軍賈嗣、魏平於祁山。

translations.literal: The following year Zhuge Liang raided Tianshui and besieged Generals Jia Si and Wei Ping at Qishan.
translations.idiomatic: Next year Zhuge Liang struck Tianshui and penned Jia Si and Wei Ping inside Qishan.

sentences.zh: 天子曰：「西方有事，非君莫可付者。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven said: “The west is in crisis—there is no one else I can entrust.”
translations.idiomatic: The court said: “Only you can shoulder the western front.”

sentences.zh: 」乃使帝西屯長安，都督雍、梁二州諸軍事，[4]統車騎將軍張郃、後將軍費曜、征蜀護軍戴淩、雍州刺史郭淮等討亮。

translations.literal: He therefore sent the Emperor to camp west at Chang’an with overall command of Yong and Liang provinces [4] and leadership over General of Chariots and Cavalry Zhang He, General of the Rear Fei Yao, Protector of the Army for the Shu Campaign Dai Ling, Inspector of Yongzhou Guo Huai, and others against Zhuge Liang.
translations.idiomatic: So he moved west to Chang’an as commander for Yong and Liang, directing Zhang He, Fei Yao, Dai Ling, Guo Huai, and the rest against Zhuge Liang.

sentences.zh: 張郃勸帝分軍住雍、郿為後鎮，帝曰：「料前軍獨能當之者，將軍言是也。

translations.literal: Zhang He urged the Emperor to divide the army and station part at Yong and Mei as a rear guard; the Emperor said: “If you judge that the van alone can hold him, general, you speak rightly.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang He proposed splitting forces between Yong and Mei as a reserve; he replied: “If the van can carry the fight alone, you are correct.

sentences.zh: 若不能當，而分為前後，此楚之三軍所以為黥布禽也。

translations.literal: But if it cannot hold and you split front from rear, that is how Chu’s three armies came to be captured by Qing Bu.”
translations.idiomatic: Split them while the front fails and you repeat Chu’s disaster at Qing Bu’s hands.”

sentences.zh: 」遂進軍隃麋。

translations.literal: He therefore advanced to Yumi.
translations.idiomatic: He pushed on to Yumi.

sentences.zh: 亮聞大軍且至，乃自帥眾將芟上邽之麥。

translations.literal: When Liang learned that the main army was approaching, he personally led his troops to reap the wheat at Shanggui.
translations.idiomatic: Hearing the host approach, Zhuge Liang himself crossed into Shanggui to strip the wheat fields.

sentences.zh: 諸將皆懼，帝曰：「亮慮多決少，必安營自固，然後芟麥，吾得二日兼行足矣。

translations.literal: The generals were alarmed; the Emperor said: “Liang deliberates endlessly yet decides rarely—he must fortify his camp before cutting grain; two days of forced marching will suffice for me.”
translations.idiomatic: His officers panicked; he said Zhuge Liang hesitates too long—he would secure camp before harvesting—so two nights’ dash would do.

sentences.zh: 」於是卷甲晨夜赴之，亮望塵而遁。

translations.literal: Thereupon they rolled up armor and raced day and night; Liang fled at the sight of their dust.
translations.idiomatic: They shed baggage and ran nonstop; Zhuge Liang bolted at their dust cloud.

sentences.zh: 帝曰：「吾倍道疲勞，此曉兵者之所貪也。

translations.literal: The Emperor said: “We have exhausted ourselves on a forced march—exactly what an army that understands war covets.
translations.idiomatic: He said: “Fatigue from speed is what seasoned troops crave.

sentences.zh: 亮不敢據渭水，此易與耳。

translations.literal: Liang dare not hold the Wei River—he will be easy to handle.”
translations.idiomatic: He will not anchor on the Wei—he is ours to manage.”

sentences.zh: 」進次漢陽，與亮相遇，帝列陣以待之。

translations.literal: He advanced to Hanyang, encountered Liang, and drew up battle lines to await him.
translations.idiomatic: He moved into Hanyang, met Zhuge Liang, and formed front against him.

sentences.zh: 使將牛金輕騎餌之，兵才接而亮退，追至祁山。

translations.literal: He ordered General Niu Jin with light cavalry to bait him; scarcely had the lines engaged when Liang withdrew, and they pursued to Qishan.
translations.idiomatic: Niu Jin’s light horse drew him out; after a brush Zhuge Liang ran and they chased all the way to Qishan.

sentences.zh: 亮屯鹵城，據南北二山，斷水為重圍。

translations.literal: Liang encamped at Lucheng, holding the northern and southern hills and cutting off the water to build layered defenses.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuge Liang walled up Lucheng between two ridges and ringed himself with cut rivers.

sentences.zh: 帝攻拔其圍，亮宵遁，追擊破之，俘斬萬計。

translations.literal: The Emperor stormed and broke his fortifications; Liang slipped away by night, was pursued and defeated, and tens of thousands were killed or captured.
translations.idiomatic: He smashed the rings; Zhuge Liang fled by dark and was chased down—dead and captured beyond count.

sentences.zh: 天子使使者勞軍，增封邑。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven dispatched envoys to reward the army and enlarged his fief.
translations.idiomatic: Imperial envoys brought rewards and added to his appanage.

sentences.zh: 時軍師杜襲、督軍薛悌皆言明年麥熟，亮必為寇，隴右無穀，宜及冬豫運。

translations.literal: At that time army adviser Du Xi and supervisor Xue Ti both said that when the wheat ripened the next year Liang would surely raid again; Longyou lacked grain and supplies ought to be moved before winter.
translations.idiomatic: Du Xi and Xue Ti warned that next harvest Zhuge Liang would return while Longyou starved—haul grain before winter.

sentences.zh: 帝曰：「亮再出祁山，一攻陳倉，挫衄而反。

translations.literal: The Emperor said: “Liang has twice emerged from Qishan and once assaulted Chencang—each time he was beaten back.
translations.idiomatic: He answered: “Twice from Qishan, once at Chencang—each time repulsed.

sentences.zh: 縱其後出，不復攻城，當求野戰，必在隴東，不在西也。

translations.literal: Even if he comes out again he will not storm cities; he will seek a field battle east of Long, not west.”
translations.idiomatic: Next time he will hunt open battle east of the Long ridges, not west.”

sentences.zh: 亮每以糧少為恨，歸必積穀，以吾料之，非三稔不能動矣。

translations.literal: Liang always lamented his shortage of grain; whenever he withdrew he stockpiled—by my reckoning he cannot move for three harvests.”
translations.idiomatic: Grain gnaws at him—every retreat piles granaries. He cannot march for three full crops.”

sentences.zh: 」於是表徙冀州農夫佃上邽，興京兆、天水、南安監冶。

translations.literal: He therefore memorialized to move tenant farmers from Ji Province up to Shanggui and to establish government foundries in Jingzhao, Tianshui, and Nan’an.
translations.idiomatic: He filed to transplant Ji farmers onto Shanggui fields and to tool imperial armories in Jingzhao, Tianshui, and Nan’an.

sentences.zh: 二年，亮又率眾十餘萬出斜谷，壘于郿之渭水南原。

translations.literal: In the second year Liang again led more than a hundred thousand men out of Xie Valley and fortified the southern bank of the Wei south of Mei.
translations.idiomatic: Year two: Zhuge Liang drove a hundred thousand through Xie Valley and dug in south of the Wei at Mei.

sentences.zh: 天子憂之，遣征蜀護軍秦朗督步騎二萬，受帝節度。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven was troubled and sent Protector of the Army for the Shu Campaign Qin Lang with twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to operate under the Emperor’s direction.
translations.idiomatic: The throne detached Qin Lang with twenty thousand foot and horse under his orders.

sentences.zh: 諸將欲住渭北以待之，帝曰：「百姓積聚皆在渭南，此必爭之地也。

translations.literal: The generals wished to stay north of the Wei and await him; the Emperor said: “The people’s stores all lie south of the river—that is ground both sides must contest.”
translations.idiomatic: They wanted the north bank; he said every barn lay south—that soil would decide the fight.

sentences.zh: 」遂引軍而濟，背水為壘。

translations.literal: He therefore led the army across and built ramparts with the river at his back.
translations.idiomatic: He crossed and stacked camps against the water.

sentences.zh: 因謂諸將曰：「亮若勇者，當出武功，依山而東。

translations.literal: He told the generals: “If Liang were bold he would exit through Wugong and wheel east along the hills.
translations.idiomatic: He lectured them: “A daring Zhuge Liang would burst from Wugong along the ridges east.

sentences.zh: 若西上五丈原，則諸軍無事矣。

translations.literal: If instead he climbs Wuzhangyuan to the west, our armies may stand idle.”
translations.idiomatic: If he climbs Wuzhangyuan westward we may barely need to stir.”

sentences.zh: 」亮果上原，將北渡渭，帝遣將軍周當屯陽遂以餌之。

translations.literal: Liang indeed climbed the plateau and prepared to cross the Wei northward; the Emperor sent General Zhou Dang to hold Yangsui as bait.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuge Liang did march onto the plateau and line up a northern crossing; Zhou Dang feigned at Yangsui.

sentences.zh: 數日，亮不動。

translations.literal: Several days passed and Liang did not move.
translations.idiomatic: Days passed without Zhuge Liang stirring.

sentences.zh: 帝曰：「亮欲爭原而不向陽遂，此意可知也。

translations.literal: The Emperor said: “He wants the high ground, not Yangsui—the intent is plain.”
translations.idiomatic: He read it: Zhuge Liang coveted the plateau, not Yangsui.

sentences.zh: 」遣將軍胡遵、雍州剌史郭淮共備陽遂，與亮會于積石。

translations.literal: He dispatched Generals Hu Zun and Inspector of Yongzhou Guo Huai jointly to secure Yangsui, and they joined Liang at Jishi.
translations.idiomatic: Hu Zun and Guo Huai sealed Yangsui and met Zhuge Liang at Jishi.

sentences.zh: 臨原而戰，亮不得進，還於五丈原。

translations.literal: They fought along the edge of the plateau; Liang could not advance and withdrew to Wuzhangyuan.
translations.idiomatic: Combat along the heights stalled Zhuge Liang and drove him back to Wuzhangyuan.

sentences.zh: 會有長星墜亮之壘，帝知其必敗，遣奇兵掎亮之後，斬五百餘級，獲生口千餘，降者六百餘人。

translations.literal: When a long comet fell on Liang’s camp the Emperor knew he was doomed; he sent unexpected troops to strike Liang’s rear, beheaded more than five hundred, captured over a thousand alive, and accepted six hundred surrenders.
translations.idiomatic: A comet struck Zhuge Liang’s camp—proof of doom—so raiders hit his rear: five hundred heads, a thousand prisoners, six hundred who yielded.

sentences.zh: 時朝廷以亮僑軍遠寇，利在急戰，每命帝持重，以候其變。

translations.literal: At that time the court held that Liang’s army was an expeditionary force operating far from home and favored forcing a quick battle; each time it ordered the Emperor to remain cautious and wait for a shift.
translations.idiomatic: Court opinion urged haste; orders told him to stay heavy-handed and watch.

sentences.zh: 亮數挑戰，帝不出，因遺帝巾幗婦人之飾。

translations.literal: Liang repeatedly challenged him to battle; the Emperor would not emerge, so Liang sent him women’s scarves and headbands as taunts.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuge Liang baited him repeatedly; he stayed quiet until women’s kerchiefs arrived.

sentences.zh: 帝怒，表請決戰，天子不許，乃遣骨鯁臣衞尉辛毗杖節為軍師以制之。

translations.literal: The Emperor angrily memorialized for a decisive engagement; the Son of Heaven forbade it and instead sent the blunt Captain of the Gate Xin Pi with imperial insignia as army adviser to restrain him.
translations.idiomatic: He demanded battle in a memorial; the emperor refused and posted Xin Pi with staff authority to leash him.

sentences.zh: 後亮復來挑戰，帝將出兵以應之，毗杖節立軍門，帝乃止。

translations.literal: Later when Liang challenged again the Emperor was about to march out to answer; Xin Pi stood staff-in-hand at the camp gate and he desisted.
translations.idiomatic: When Zhuge Liang tried again he nearly rode out—Xin Pi blocked the gate with his baton until he stopped.

sentences.zh: 初，蜀將姜維聞毗來，謂亮曰：「辛毗杖節而至，賊不復出矣。

translations.literal: Earlier, when Shu general Jiang Wei heard that Xin Pi had come, he told Liang: “Xin Pi arrives with credentials—the enemy will not come forth again.”
translations.idiomatic: Jiang Wei had warned: “Xin Pi means no more field battles.”

sentences.zh: 」亮曰：「彼本無戰心，所以固請者，以示武于其眾耳。

translations.literal: Liang said: “They have no real wish to fight; their insistence on requesting battle is only to put martial spirit on display before their troops.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuge Liang answered: “They seek spectacle, not steel—they parade martial theater for the ranks.

sentences.zh: 將在軍，君命有所不受，苟能制吾，豈千里而請戰邪！」

translations.literal: A general in the field may reject orders from his ruler; if they could truly pin me down, why would they memorialize for battle from a thousand li away!”
translations.idiomatic: Field commanders ignore distant edicts—if they could trap me they would not beg Luoyang for permission!”

sentences.zh: 帝弟孚書問軍事，帝復書曰：「亮志大而不見機，多謀而少決，好兵而無權，雖提卒十萬，巳墮吾畫中，破之必矣。

translations.literal: The Emperor’s younger brother Fu wrote asking about the campaign; the Emperor answered: “Liang’s ambitions are vast yet he misses his moment; he schemes much but decides little; he loves soldiering yet lacks flexibility—though he leads a hundred thousand men he has already fallen into my design and will surely be broken.”
translations.idiomatic: Sima Fu’s letter drew a cool reply: Zhuge Liang dreams large but times poorly, hesitates in crisis, loves battle without adaptability—the hundred thousand were already snared.

sentences.zh: 」與之對壘百餘日，會亮病卒，諸將燒營遁走，百姓奔告，帝出兵追之。

translations.literal: After opposing him for more than a hundred days, Liang died of illness; his generals burned the camps and fled, the people ran to report it, and the Emperor sent troops in pursuit.
translations.idiomatic: A hundred days of stalemate ended when Zhuge Liang died—his men torched camp and bolted, civilians brought word, and pursuit followed.

sentences.zh: 亮長史楊儀反旗鳴鼓，若將距帝者。

translations.literal: Liang’s chief clerk Yang Yi reversed the banners and beat the drums as if preparing to resist the Emperor.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Yi feigned a counterattack—flags reversed, drums thundering.

sentences.zh: 帝以窮寇不之逼，於是楊儀結陣而去。

translations.literal: The Emperor would not press a cornered enemy; Yang Yi therefore formed ranks and withdrew.
translations.idiomatic: He refused to harry a desperate foe, so Yang Yi marched away in order.

sentences.zh: 經日，乃行其營壘，觀其遺事，獲其圖書、糧穀甚眾。

translations.literal: After a full day he entered their fortifications, inspected what they had left behind, and captured a great quantity of maps, documents, and grain.
translations.idiomatic: Next day he walked the abandoned works and seized maps, papers, and grain in heaps.

sentences.zh: 帝審其必死，曰：「天下奇才也。

translations.literal: The Emperor examined the evidence and knew Liang must be dead, saying: “A peerless talent under Heaven.”
translations.idiomatic: The debris told him Zhuge Liang was dead—truly a genius of the age.

sentences.zh: 」辛毗以為尚未可知。

translations.literal: Xin Pi thought the matter still uncertain.
translations.idiomatic: Xin Pi still urged caution.

sentences.zh: 帝曰：「軍家所重，軍書密計、兵馬糧穀，今皆棄之，豈有人捐其五藏而可以生乎？

translations.literal: The Emperor said: “What armies prize—secret plans, tallies, horses, and grain—they have all cast aside; can a man cast aside his five viscera and still live?
translations.idiomatic: He shot back: armies do not abandon cipher books, tallies, horses, and grain unless the commander is gone—could anyone shed vital organs and breathe?

sentences.zh: 宜急追之。

translations.literal: We should pursue at once.
translations.idiomatic: Pursue now.

sentences.zh: 」關中多蒺䔧，帝使軍士二千人著軟材平底木屐前行，蒺藜悉著屐，然後馬步俱進。

translations.literal: Guanzhong was thick with caltrops; the Emperor had two thousand soldiers put on soft wooden clogs with flat soles and walk ahead; the caltrops stuck to the clogs, after which cavalry and infantry advanced together.
translations.idiomatic: Guanzhong bristled with caltrops—two thousand men in wooden clogs swept the path clear for horse and foot.

sentences.zh: 追到赤岸，乃知亮死審問。

translations.literal: They pursued to Red Shore (Chì’àn) and only then confirmed beyond doubt that Liang was dead.
translations.idiomatic: Only at Red Shore did rumor harden into fact.

sentences.zh: 時百姓為之諺曰：「死諸葛走生仲達。

translations.literal: The common folk composed a rhyme: “A dead Zhuge drove off a living Zhongda.”
translations.idiomatic: People sang: “The dead Zhuge ran off the living Zhongda.”

sentences.zh: 」帝聞而笑曰：「吾便料生，不便料死故也。」

translations.literal: When the Emperor heard it he laughed and said: “I could judge him alive; I could not judge him dead—that is all.”
translations.idiomatic: He laughed: “I could read him breathing; I could not read him cold—that was my blind spot.”

sentences.zh: 先是，亮使至，帝問曰：「諸葛公起居何如，食可幾米？

translations.literal: Earlier, when an envoy from Liang arrived, the Emperor asked: “How is Lord Zhuge’s health, and how many sheng of rice does he eat?
translations.idiomatic: Earlier he had asked Liang’s envoy how Zhuge Liang slept and how many sheng of rice he ate.

sentences.zh: 」[5]對曰：「三四升。

translations.literal: He answered [5]: “Three or four sheng.”
translations.idiomatic: The reply: three or four sheng per meal.

sentences.zh: 」次問政事，曰：「二十罰已上皆自省覽。

translations.literal: He next asked about administration and was told: “All punishments of twenty strokes or more he reviews personally.”
translations.idiomatic: On administration: every flogging above twenty strokes crossed his own desk.

sentences.zh: 」帝既而告人曰：「諸葛孔明其能久乎！

translations.literal: The Emperor afterward told others: “How long can Kongming last!”
translations.idiomatic: He later muttered that Kongming could not endure such pace.

sentences.zh: 」竟如其言。

translations.literal: Events proved him right.
translations.idiomatic: Time proved him right.

sentences.zh: 亮部將楊儀、魏延爭權，儀斬延，并其眾。

translations.literal: Liang’s officers Yang Yi and Wei Yan struggled for power; Yi executed Yan and absorbed his troops.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Yi murdered Wei Yan and seized his command.

sentences.zh: 帝欲乘隙而進，有詔不許。

translations.literal: The Emperor wished to exploit the opening and advance, but an edict forbade it.
translations.idiomatic: He itched to strike the chaos; an imperial veto stopped him.

sentences.zh: 三年，遷太尉，累增封邑。

translations.literal: In the third year he was promoted to Grand Commandant and his fief was repeatedly enlarged.
translations.idiomatic: Third year: Grand Commandant, with fiefs piled higher.

sentences.zh: 蜀將馬岱入寇，帝遣將軍牛金擊走之，斬千餘級。

translations.literal: Shu general Ma Dai raided the border; the Emperor sent General Niu Jin to drive him off and beheaded more than a thousand.
translations.idiomatic: Ma Dai of Shu raided in; Niu Jin threw him back with a thousand heads.

sentences.zh: 武都氐王苻雙、強端帥其屬六千餘人來降。

translations.literal: The Di kings of Wudu, Fu Shuang and Qiang Duan, led more than six thousand of their followers to surrender.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Shuang and Qiang Duan of Wudu Di brought six thousand followers in.

translations.literal: Six.
translations.idiomatic: Six.

sentences.zh: 關東饑，帝運長安粟五百萬斛輸於京師。

translations.literal: East of the passes suffered famine; the Emperor shipped five million hu of grain from Chang’an to the capital.
translations.idiomatic: Famine east of the passes—five million hu moved from Chang’an to Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 四年，獲白鹿，獻之。

translations.literal: In the fourth year a white deer was captured and presented.
translations.idiomatic: Fourth year: hunters presented a white deer.

sentences.zh: 天子曰：「昔周公旦輔成王，有素雉之貢。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven said: “Anciently the Duke of Zhou aided King Cheng and offered a plain-colored pheasant as tribute.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor cited Zhou Gong’s white pheasant for King Cheng.

sentences.zh: 今君受陝西之任，有白鹿之獻，豈非忠誠協符，千載同契，俾乂邦家，以永厥休邪！」

translations.literal: Now you hold responsibility for Shaanxi and present a white deer—is this not loyalty answering Heaven’s sign, a pact spanning a thousand years that will bring peace to the state and eternal blessing!”
translations.idiomatic: Now you guard Shaanxi with the same omen—a white deer sealing loyalty across ages.

sentences.zh: 及遼東太守公孫文懿反，徵帝詣京師。

translations.literal: When Liaodong Prefect Gongsun Yuan rebelled, the Emperor was summoned to the capital.
translations.idiomatic: Gongsun Yuan’s revolt pulled him to Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 天子曰：「此不足以勞君，事欲必克，故以相煩耳。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven said: “This ought not tax you, yet we must win absolutely—therefore we trouble you.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor apologized: victory had to be certain—that meant bothering him.

sentences.zh: 君度其作何計？

translations.literal: What stratagem do you estimate he will adopt?”
translations.idiomatic: What gambit did he expect?

sentences.zh: 」對曰：「棄城預走，上計也。

translations.literal: He replied: “Abandon the city and flee beforehand—that is the best plan.”
translations.idiomatic: Best case: abandon Liaodong and run early.

sentences.zh: 據遼水以距大軍，次計也。

translations.literal: Hold the Liao River to block the main army—that is the middling plan.”
translations.idiomatic: Middle course: defend the Liao line.

sentences.zh: 坐守襄平，此成擒耳。

translations.literal: Sit and defend Xiangping—then he is merely waiting to be captured.”
translations.idiomatic: Worst: hide inside Xiangping and await capture.

sentences.zh: 」天子曰：「其計將安出？

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven said: “How then will his plan unfold?”
translations.idiomatic: The emperor asked how it would play out.

sentences.zh: 」對曰：「惟明者能深度彼己，豫有所棄，此非其所及也。

translations.literal: He replied: “Only the enlightened can measure friend and foe deeply and discard options in advance—this enemy cannot reach that.”
translations.idiomatic: Only a sage weighs both sides and sacrifices pieces ahead—Yuan cannot.

sentences.zh: 今懸軍遠征，將謂不能持久，必先距遼水而後守，此中下計也。

translations.literal: Now our army is isolated on a distant expedition; he will suppose we cannot endure long and will certainly hold the Liao River first and then defend—that is the middle or lower plan.”
translations.idiomatic: An isolated host looks fragile; Yuan will cling to the river—that middling strategy.

sentences.zh: 」天子曰：「往還幾時？

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven said: “How long will the round trip take?”
translations.idiomatic: The emperor pressed for a timetable.

sentences.zh: 」對曰：「往百日，還百日，攻百日，以六十日為休息，一年足矣。」

translations.literal: He replied: “Outbound one hundred days, return one hundred days, assault one hundred days, with sixty days set aside for rest—one year suffices.”
translations.idiomatic: He answered: “March out a hundred days, come back a hundred, fight a hundred, rest sixty—that fills a year.”

sentences.zh: 是時大修宮室，加之以軍旅，百姓饑弊。

translations.literal: At that time palace construction was greatly expanded and military campaigns piled on; the common people were hungry and exhausted.
translations.idiomatic: Court architects ran wild while armies marched—the people starved under both burdens.

sentences.zh: 帝將即戎，乃諫曰：「昔周公營洛邑，蕭何造未央，今宮室未備，臣之責也。

translations.literal: The Emperor was about to take the field and remonstrated: “Anciently the Duke of Zhou built Luoyi and Xiao He raised Weiyang—today the palaces remain unfinished; that fault is mine.
translations.idiomatic: As he prepared to march he urged restraint: incomplete Luoyang palaces were his ministers’ shame—the builders had failed the throne.

sentences.zh: 然自河以北，百姓困窮，外內有役，勢不並興，宜假絕內務，以救時急。」

translations.literal: Yet north of the Yellow River the people are destitute; inner and outer burdens cannot both rise—we ought to suspend inner court projects to answer pressing need.”
translations.idiomatic: North of the river peasants were ruined; palaces and armies could not rise together—pause vanity works and feed the hour.”

sentences.zh: 景初二年，帥牛金、胡遵等步騎四萬，發自京都。

translations.literal: In the second year of Jingchu (238) he led Niu Jin, Hu Zun, and others with forty thousand infantry and cavalry out of the capital.
translations.idiomatic: Jingchu year two: forty thousand horse and foot under Niu Jin and Hu Zun left Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 車駕送出西明門，詔弟孚、子師送過溫，賜以穀帛牛酒，敕郡守典農以下皆往會焉。

translations.literal: The imperial carriage escorted him through the Ximing Gate; an edict ordered his younger brother Fu and son Shi to see him past Wen, awarding grain, silk, cattle, and wine, and commanded the prefect and agricultural director downward to assemble.
translations.idiomatic: The sovereign rode to Ximing; Fu and Shi escorted him home to Wen with sacks of grain, silk rolls, oxen, and wine while every county clerk was told to turn out.

sentences.zh: 見父老故舊，讌飲累日。

translations.literal: He met elders and old friends and feasted for days on end.
translations.idiomatic: He lingered with hometown elders over cups for night after night.

sentences.zh: 帝歎息，悵然有感，為歌曰：「天地開闢，日月重光。

translations.literal: The Emperor sighed, melancholy stirring him, and sang: “Heaven and earth were opened; sun and moon shine anew.
translations.idiomatic: He composed a marching song—creation renewed, daylight reborn.

sentences.zh: 遭遇際會，畢力遐方。

translations.literal: Meeting his destined hour, he pours every strength into distant lands.
translations.idiomatic: Seizing the moment he spends his force on far frontiers.

sentences.zh: 將掃羣穢，還過故鄉。

translations.literal: He will sweep away every stain and pass once more through his native place.
translations.idiomatic: He would scour the realm clean and ride again through old Wen lanes.

sentences.zh: 肅清萬里，總齊八荒。

translations.literal: Purifying ten thousand li, bringing the eight wastes under one rule.
translations.idiomatic: Ten thousand li made pure; the wastelands marshaled as one.

sentences.zh: 告成歸老，待罪舞陽。

translations.literal: Having reported success he retires old to await judgment at Wuyang.”
translations.idiomatic: Victory reported, he would retire to Wuyang and answer for his charge.”

sentences.zh: 」遂進師，經孤竹，越碣石，次于遼水。

translations.literal: Thereupon he advanced the army, passed Guzhu, crossed Jieshi, and halted at the Liao River.
translations.idiomatic: The columns rolled past Guzhu and Jieshi to the Liao.

sentences.zh: 文懿果遣步騎數萬，阻遼隧，堅壁而守，南北六七十里，以距帝。

translations.literal: Wenyi indeed sent several tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry to block Liaosui, fortifying walls and holding sixty or seventy li north to south against the Emperor.
translations.idiomatic: Gongsun Yuan plugged Liaosui with tens of thousands—palisades stretched seventy li along the narrows.

sentences.zh: 帝盛兵多張旗幟出其南，賊盡銳赴之。

translations.literal: The Emperor massed troops and unfurled many banners south of them; the rebels committed every elite regiment there.
translations.idiomatic: Sima Yi feigned strength on the southern bank and drew the Liaodong army off.

sentences.zh: 乃泛舟潛濟以出其北，與賊營相逼，沈舟焚梁，傍遼水作長圍，棄賊而向襄平。

translations.literal: He then floated boats and secretly crossed to their north, pressing against their camp—sank boats, burned bridges, threw a long cordon along the Liao, abandoned the enemy column, and marched on Xiangping.
translations.idiomatic: Under cover of dark water he slipped upstream, burned the crossings, pinned the Liao with earthworks, and ignored the camp for Xiangping.

sentences.zh: 諸將言曰：「不攻賊而作圍，非所以示眾也。

translations.literal: The generals said: “Instead of striking the enemy we build a perimeter—this shows no authority to the army.”
translations.idiomatic: His officers protested: siege lines without battle looked weak.

sentences.zh: 」帝曰：「賊堅營高壘，欲以老吾兵也。

translations.literal: The Emperor said: “The enemy locks tight ramparts wishing to wear down our troops.
translations.idiomatic: He answered: “They wall up to exhaust us.

sentences.zh: 攻之，正入其計，此王邑所以恥過昆陽也。

translations.literal: To assault them plays straight into their plan—that is why Wang Yi was disgraced beyond Kunyang.
translations.idiomatic: Storming those walls repeats Wang Yi’s humiliation at Kunyang.

sentences.zh: 古人曰，敵雖高壘，不得不與我戰者，攻其所必救也。

translations.literal: The ancients said: though the foe piles high ramparts, we can force battle when we strike what he must rescue.
translations.idiomatic: Classics teach—strike the rescue point and even high walls must open.

sentences.zh: 賊大眾在此，則巢窟虛矣。

translations.literal: Their main host stands here—then their nest lies empty.
translations.idiomatic: Their veterans cling here while Xiangping lies naked.

sentences.zh: 我直指襄平，則人懷內懼，懼而求戰，破之必矣。

translations.literal: If we strike straight at Xiangping, hearts within will fear; fear drives them to battle—then destruction is certain.”
translations.idiomatic: A thrust at Xiangping panics the capital and flushes them out—that ends it.”

sentences.zh: 」遂整陣而過。

translations.literal: Thereupon he dressed ranks and marched through.
translations.idiomatic: He aligned divisions and slipped past.

sentences.zh: 賊見兵出其後，果邀之。

translations.literal: When the rebels saw troops emerge behind them they indeed tried to intercept.
translations.idiomatic: The Liaodong army wheeled about to cut him off.

sentences.zh: 帝謂諸將曰：「所以不攻其營，正欲致此，不可失也。

translations.literal: The Emperor told the generals: “The reason we did not assault their camp was precisely to produce this—we must not lose the chance.”
translations.idiomatic: He reminded them the feint was bait—do not waste the trap.

sentences.zh: 」乃縱兵逆擊，大破之，三戰皆捷。

translations.literal: He then unleashed troops in a counterattack and shattered them; three engagements brought three victories.
translations.idiomatic: He hurled the lines forward and routed them thrice running.

sentences.zh: 賊保襄平，進軍圍之。

translations.literal: The rebels held Xiangping; he advanced and invested it.
translations.idiomatic: They fled inside Xiangping; he tightened the ring.

sentences.zh: 初，文懿聞魏師之出也，請救於孫權。

translations.literal: Earlier, when Wenyi heard the Wei army had marched, he begged rescue from Sun Quan.
translations.idiomatic: Gongsun Yuan had cried to Sun Quan when Wei stirred.

sentences.zh: 權亦出兵遙為之聲援，遺文懿書曰：「司馬公善用兵，變化若神，所向無前，深為弟憂之。」

translations.literal: Quan also sent troops from afar as vocal support and wrote Wenyi: “Lord Sima excels at arms—his shifts are godlike, none withstand his advance—I deeply fear for you, younger brother.”
translations.idiomatic: Wu dispatched a distant demonstration and warned Yuan: Sima Yi reads war like a spirit—nothing survives his front—I tremble for you, brother.

sentences.zh: 會霖潦，大水平地數尺，三軍恐，欲移營。

translations.literal: Seasonal rains poured; floodwaters stood several chi deep on level ground; the three armies feared and wished to shift camp.
translations.idiomatic: Monsoon floods drowned the plain; men clamored to move.

sentences.zh: 帝令軍中敢有言徙者斬。

translations.literal: The Emperor ordered that whoever spoke of relocating be executed.
translations.idiomatic: He threatened death for talk of redeployment.

sentences.zh: 都督令史張靜犯令，斬之，軍中乃定。

translations.literal: Supervisory clerk Zhang Jing violated the order and was beheaded—only then did the army steady.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Jing broke the rule and lost his head—the ranks fell silent.

sentences.zh: 賊恃水，樵牧自若。

translations.literal: The rebels trusted the water and gathered firewood and grazed cattle as usual.
translations.idiomatic: The defenders still sent out woodcutters as if dry.

sentences.zh: 諸將欲取之，皆不聽。

translations.literal: The generals wished to seize those parties; he forbade every proposal.
translations.idiomatic: Staff urged raids on foragers; he refused each time.

sentences.zh: 司馬陳珪曰：「昔攻上庸，八部並進，晝夜不息，故能一旬之半，拔堅城，斬孟達。

translations.literal: Marshal Chen Gui said: “When we invested Shangyong eight columns advanced together without pause day or night—therefore in half a ten-day span we took the stronghold and beheaded Meng Da.
translations.idiomatic: Chen Gui recalled Shangyong—eight prongs, no sleep, Meng Da dead in five days.

sentences.zh: 今者遠來而更安緩，愚竊惑焉。

translations.literal: Now we have marched far yet act leisurely—I privately am baffled.”
translations.idiomatic: This siege crawls—I cannot fathom it.”

sentences.zh: 」帝曰：「孟達眾少而食支一年，吾將士四倍于達而糧不淹月，以一月圖一年，安可不速？

translations.literal: The Emperor said: “Meng Da had few troops but grain for a year; our officers and men outnumbered him fourfold yet provisions lasted less than a month—with one month against a year, how could we not race?
translations.idiomatic: He said Meng Da starved while holding a year’s grain; Wei had four times his numbers but less than a month of rice—speed was survival.

sentences.zh: 以四擊一，正令半解，猶當為之。

translations.literal: Four strikes one—even were half to dissolve we still had to try.
translations.idiomatic: Odds four-to-one meant half might melt yet we still gambled.

sentences.zh: 是以不計死傷，與糧競也。

translations.literal: Therefore we did not count casualties but raced grain supplies.”
translations.idiomatic: We traded blood for calendar days.”

sentences.zh: 今賊眾我寡，賊飢我飽，水雨乃爾，功力不設，雖當促之，亦何所為。

translations.literal: Now they outnumber us yet we are full while they hunger—the rains leave no dry footing—even if we pressed, what could we gain?
translations.idiomatic: Today they swarm yet starve while we eat—the mud stalls engines—forcing gains nothing.

sentences.zh: 自發京師，不憂賊攻，但恐賊走。

translations.literal: Since leaving the capital I have not feared that the rebels would attack—only that they would flee.
translations.idiomatic: Since Luoyang I dreaded flight, not assault.

sentences.zh: 今賊糧垂盡，而圍落未合，掠其牛馬，抄其樵采，此故驅之走也。

translations.literal: Now their grain nears exhaustion yet our siege ring is unclosed—plunder cattle and raid firewood crews—that truly drives them to run.
translations.idiomatic: Let them drain granaries while our cordon gapes—steal oxen, harass fuel parties—that stampsede them.

sentences.zh: 夫兵者詭道，善因事變。

translations.literal: War is the path of deception—the adept ride circumstance.
translations.idiomatic: Combat is deceit; bend each twist.

sentences.zh: 賊憑眾恃雨，故雖飢困，未肯束手，當示無能以安之。

translations.literal: The rebels rely on numbers and trust the rains—therefore though hungry and trapped they will not bind hands willingly—we should display helplessness to soothe them.
translations.idiomatic: They lean on rain and bodies—starving, they still refuse ropes—feign weakness.

sentences.zh: 取小利以驚之。

translations.literal: Snatching petty gains alarms them.
translations.idiomatic: Small raids only wake them.

sentences.zh: 非計也。

translations.literal: That is not the stratagem.”
translations.idiomatic: That would spoil the snare.”

sentences.zh: 」朝廷聞師遇雨，咸請召還。

translations.literal: The court heard the army met rain and all petitioned recall.
translations.idiomatic: Luoyang heard mud and demanded withdrawal.

sentences.zh: 天子曰：「司馬公臨危制變，計日擒之矣。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven said: “Lord Sima masters crisis and bends fate—count the days and he will seize them.”
translations.idiomatic: The emperor answered: Sima Yi thrives in chaos—he will bag Yuan on schedule.

sentences.zh: 」既而雨止，遂合圍。

translations.literal: Soon the rain stopped and they completed the cordon.
translations.idiomatic: Skies cleared; the ring closed.

sentences.zh: 起土山地道，楯櫓鉤橦，發矢石雨下，晝夜攻之。

translations.literal: They piled earth hills and dug tunnels—shields, rams, hooks—arrows and stones rained in assault day and night.
translations.idiomatic: They stacked siege mounds, bored mines, and hailed stone until the walls shook.

sentences.zh: 時有長星，色白，有芒鬣，自襄平城西南流于東北，墜於梁水，城中震慴。

translations.literal: At that time a long comet appeared, white with bristling rays, flowing from southwest of Xiangping toward northeast, falling into the Liang River—the city shook with terror.
translations.idiomatic: A white comet streaked from Xiangping’s southwest to the Liang—terror seized the town.

sentences.zh: 文懿大懼，乃使其所署相國王建、御史大夫柳甫乞降，請解圍面縛。

translations.literal: Wenyi was terrified and sent his appointed Chancellor Wang Jian and Imperial Counselor Liu Fu to beg surrender, asking to lift the siege so he could bind himself.
translations.idiomatic: Yuan sent Wang Jian and Liu Fu pleading for the siege to lift so he could come out with bound hands.

sentences.zh: 不許，執建等，皆斬之。

translations.literal: He did not consent—seized Jian and the others and executed them all.
translations.idiomatic: Sima Yi refused—seized the envoys and took their heads.

sentences.zh: 檄告文懿曰：「昔楚鄭列國，而鄭伯猶肉袒牽羊而迎之。

translations.literal: He proclaimed to Wenyi: “Anciently Chu and Zheng were peer kingdoms yet the Earl of Zheng still bared breast and led sheep to welcome.
translations.idiomatic: His bulletin cited ancient Zheng greeting Chu with stripped chest and sheep.

sentences.zh: 孤為王人，位則上公，而建等欲孤解圍退舍，豈楚鄭之謂邪！

translations.literal: I am the king’s minister, rank equals supreme duke—yet Jian and others ask me to lift siege and withdraw—is this Chu and Zheng’s etiquette!
translations.idiomatic: He held kingly mandate at senior duke rank—yet they ordered him aside like a treaty foe.

sentences.zh: 二人老耄，必傳言失旨，已相為斬之。

translations.literal: Those two are aged dotards—they must have garbled the terms—I have executed them accordingly.
translations.idiomatic: Two senile mouthpieces mis-spoke—he killed both.

sentences.zh: 若意有未已，可更遣年少有明決者來。

translations.literal: If intent remains unfinished, send younger men with firm resolve.”
translations.idiomatic: Need another plea—send sharp youths.”

sentences.zh: 」文懿復遣侍中衞演乞剋日送任。

translations.literal: Wenyi again sent attendant Wei Yan requesting a fixed day to deliver hostages.
translations.idiomatic: Yuan tried again—Wei Yan begging a hostage deadline.

sentences.zh: 帝謂演曰：「軍事大要有五，能戰當戰，不能戰當守，不能守當走，餘二事惟有降與死耳。

translations.literal: The Emperor told Yan: “The great essentials of warfare number five: if you can fight, fight; if not, defend; if not, flee—the remaining two paths are surrender or death.
translations.idiomatic: He lectured Yan on war’s pentad—fight, hold, run, yield, die.

sentences.zh: 汝不肯面縛，此為決就死也，不須送任。

translations.literal: You refuse to bind yourself—that means you choose death; hostages are needless.”
translations.idiomatic: Refusing bonds chooses death—skip hostages.”

sentences.zh: 」文懿攻南圍突出，帝縱兵擊敗之，斬于梁水之上星墜之所。

translations.literal: Wenyi assaulted the southern siege line trying to break out; the Emperor unleashed troops, defeated him, and beheaded him at the spot where the star fell above the Liang River.
translations.idiomatic: Yuan rammed the southern sector; Sima Yi crushed him and struck off his head where the comet had plunged.

sentences.zh: 既入城，立兩標以別新舊焉。

translations.literal: After entering the city he erected two markers to separate new guilt from old inhabitants.
translations.idiomatic: Inside the walls twin posts marked who belonged to the revolt.

sentences.zh: 男子年十五已上七千餘人皆殺之，以為京觀。

translations.literal: All males fifteen sui and older—more than seven thousand—were executed to form a burial mound.
translations.idiomatic: Seven thousand males above fifteen died for the victory mound.

sentences.zh: 偽公卿已下皆伏誅，戮其將軍畢盛等二千餘人。

translations.literal: All false dukes and ministers downward were executed; more than two thousand including general Bi Sheng were put to death.
translations.idiomatic: Phony ministers died with two thousand officers including Bi Sheng.

sentences.zh: 收戶四萬，口三十餘萬。

translations.literal: Households registered numbered forty thousand; mouths exceeded three hundred thousand.
translations.idiomatic: Registers captured forty thousand households and three hundred thousand people.

sentences.zh: 初，文懿篡其叔父恭位而囚之。

translations.literal: Earlier Wenyi had usurped his uncle Gong’s position and imprisoned him.
translations.idiomatic: Yuan had seized Uncle Gong’s seat and jailed him.

sentences.zh: 及將反，將軍綸直、賈範等苦諫，文懿皆殺之。

translations.literal: When about to rebel generals Lun Zhi and Jia Fan remonstrated bitterly—Wenyi executed them all.
translations.idiomatic: On the eve of revolt Lun Zhi and Jia Fan pleaded—Yuan murdered them.

sentences.zh: 帝乃釋恭之囚，封直等之墓，顯其遺嗣。

translations.literal: The Emperor then released Gong from prison, tended the tombs of Zhi and others, and honored their surviving heirs.
translations.idiomatic: Sima Yi freed Gong, rebuilt martyrs’ graves, and ennobled their sons.

sentences.zh: 令曰：「古之伐國，誅其鯨鯢而已，諸為文懿所詿誤者，皆原之。

translations.literal: His order said: “Anciently attacking a state executed only the great villains—all misled by Wenyi are forgiven.
translations.idiomatic: His edict spared everyone Yuan had duped—execute whales alone.

sentences.zh: 中國人欲還舊鄉，恣聽之。」

translations.literal: Chinese who wish to return to former homes—go as they please.”
translations.idiomatic: Han subjects longing for old hearths may depart freely.”

sentences.zh: 時有兵士寒凍，乞襦，帝弗之與。

translations.literal: At that time soldiers freezing in the cold begged for padded jackets; the Emperor did not grant them.
translations.idiomatic: Frozen troops begged quilts; he withheld them.

sentences.zh: 或曰：「幸多故襦，可以賜之。

translations.literal: Someone said: “There are many surplus jackets—they may be distributed.”
translations.idiomatic: Aides noted warehouses bulged with coats.

sentences.zh: 」帝曰：「襦者官物，人臣無私施也。

translations.literal: The Emperor said: “Padded garments are state property—a minister may not give private largesse.”
translations.idiomatic: Official cloth stays official—ministers do not play philanthropist.

sentences.zh: 」乃奏軍人年六十已上者罷遣千餘人，將吏從軍死亡者致喪還家。

translations.literal: He then memorialized to discharge over a thousand soldiers aged sixty and above and to send home the remains of officers who died on campaign.
translations.idiomatic: He cashiered thousand greybeards and shipped coffins west.

sentences.zh: 遂班師。

translations.literal: Thereupon he withdrew the army.
translations.idiomatic: Then he marched home.

sentences.zh: 天子遣使者勞軍于薊，增封食昆陽，并前二縣。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven dispatched envoys to reward the army at Ji, enlarged the grain income with Kunyang, together with the previous two counties.
translations.idiomatic: Envoys met him at Ji with fresh fiefs—Kunyang added to two older counties.

sentences.zh: 初，帝至襄平，夢天子枕其膝，曰：「視吾面。

translations.literal: Earlier when the Emperor reached Xiangping he dreamed the Son of Heaven rested his head on the Emperor’s knees, saying: “Look upon my face.
translations.idiomatic: At Xiangping he dreamed the emperor’s head lay in his lap—Look at me.

sentences.zh: 」俛視有異於常，心惡之。

translations.literal: Stooping to look it differed from the ordinary—his heart reviled it.
translations.idiomatic: The face looked wrong—he woke uneasy.

sentences.zh: 先是，詔帝便道鎮關中；

translations.literal: Earlier an edict had ordered the Emperor by convenient route to hold Guanzhong;
translations.idiomatic: Orders already told him to guard Guanzhong by detour.

sentences.zh: 及次白屋，有詔召帝，三日之間，詔書五至。

translations.literal: When halting at Baiwu edicts summoned the Emperor—within three days five edicts arrived.
translations.idiomatic: At Baiwu five summons arrived in three days.

sentences.zh: 手詔曰：「間側息望到，到便直排閤入，視吾面。

translations.literal: A handwritten edict said: “I lean sideways longing for your arrival—when you arrive enter straight through the gate and look upon my face.
translations.idiomatic: Imperial brush ordered him through the doors at once—look at my face.

sentences.zh: 」帝大遽，乃乘追鋒車晝夜兼行，自白屋四百餘里，一宿而至。

translations.literal: The Emperor was greatly alarmed and rode the pursuit-chariot day and night—more than four hundred li from Baiwu, arriving in one night.
translations.idiomatic: Panic drove the relay carriage four hundred li overnight.

sentences.zh: 引入嘉福殿臥內，升御牀。

translations.literal: He was conducted into the Jiafu Palace inner chamber and helped onto the imperial couch.
translations.idiomatic: Eunuchs led him to Jiafu’s bedchamber and the throne couch.

sentences.zh: 帝流涕問疾，天子執帝手，目齊王曰：「以後事相託。

translations.literal: The Emperor wept asking after illness; the Son of Heaven grasped the Emperor’s hand, eyes on Prince Qi, saying: “I entrust what follows to you.
translations.idiomatic: Weeping at bedside, Cao Fang clasped his arm—Qi Prince watched—my aftermath is yours.

sentences.zh: 死乃復可忍，吾忍死待君，得相見，無所復恨矣。

translations.literal: Death then could still be endured—I endured death awaiting you; having met face to face I lack further regret.”
translations.idiomatic: I clung to life for this audience—now death is bearable.”

sentences.zh: 」與大將軍曹爽並受遺詔輔少主。

translations.literal: Together with Grand General Cao Shuang he received testamentary edicts to aid the young lord.
translations.idiomatic: He and Cao Shuang sealed regency for the boy emperor.

sentences.zh: 正始元年春正月，[7]東倭重譯納貢，焉耆、危須諸國，弱水以南，鮮卑名王，皆遣使來獻。

translations.literal: First month of spring in the first year of Zhengshi [7]—Wa envoys through interpreters presented tribute; Yanqi, Weixu, lands south of Ruoshui, Xianbei titled kings—all sent envoys with offerings.
translations.idiomatic: Zhengshi spring month one [7]—Japanese interpreters, Yanqi, southerners beyond Ruoshui, Xianbei chiefs—all brought gifts.

sentences.zh: 天子歸美宰輔，又增帝封邑。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven attributed glory to the chief ministers and again enlarged the Emperor’s fief.
translations.idiomatic: The court credited the ministers and fattened Sima Yi’s lands.

sentences.zh: 初，魏明帝好修宮室，制度靡麗，百姓苦之。

translations.literal: Earlier Wei Mingdi loved constructing palaces—standards extravagant—the common people suffered.
translations.idiomatic: Mingdi’s terraces had bled the people.

sentences.zh: 帝自遼東還，役者猶萬餘人，雕玩之物動以千計。

translations.literal: When the Emperor returned from Liaodong laborers still numbered over ten thousand; carved trinkets mounted by thousands.
translations.idiomatic: Ten thousand corvée hands still carved gewgaws by the thousand.

sentences.zh: 至是皆奏罷之，節用務農，天下欣賴焉。

translations.literal: At this point all were memorialized to cease—economizing and promoting farming—the realm rejoiced and relied on him.
translations.idiomatic: He stopped the yards, urged ploughs—the empire sighed relief.

sentences.zh: 二年夏五月，吳將全琮寇芍陂，朱然、孫倫圍樊城，諸葛瑾、步騭掠柤中，帝請自討之。
